Yes, there are. But the question is about phones, not encryption schemes.

You can use the best encryption method in the world- probably some multiple layer thing that involves Serpent (such as AES-Twofish-Serpent, offered by veracrypt), but if your password is 5531, it will be brute forced in seconds. Most phone encryption is ultimately all unlocked by a tiny little thing with no meaningful entropy.

The phone manufacturers all use hardware to guard this. The high level thing is, there's a tiny piece of hardware that is meant to be impossible to read the data from, which is supposed to both take the trivial passcode in common use and output either the key or something that the OS or an attacker could use to find the key, AND ALSO to track the number of tries. After enough tries, it can simply delete whatever it has inside that can generate the key.

This means that these phones are all ultimately guarded by very hard to manipulate hardware, but you should never assume this is out of the grasp of state actors.

Lets say you are aware of this, and you assume that this piece of hardware will be worked around by your adversaries, so you choose a cryptographically secure passphrase- perhaps a small poem that you wrote, or abbreviations from a phrase, or some garble of numbers, letters, and specials that is a massive pain. You have to enter this every time you try to log in to your phone, and you have increased your security... but is it to the same degree that something like Veracrypt or LUKS would give you? The answer is, we just don't know, because that little hardware thing still knows stuff about your key that a regular computer without such a device doesn't know. It could be possible to read that thing's state via a really clever method, and that could, depending on how it is implemented, mean that your secure passphrase effectively has hints inside of it.

A phone will never be as secure for keeping your thoughts private as something on your hard drive that only relies on software to keep things secure because of this uncertainty. The phone manufacturers- many of them at least- are trying. Apple is trying to make their secure enclave as close to perfect as they can. Some of the top Androids are as well. I'm not sure what path Purism will be able to afford to take, but you can bet they value privacy highly as well.

But at the end of the day, you KNOW your data is not secure if you use anything with low entropy- a four or six digit PIN, a thumbprint, a facial image. It only has a chance of security if you use passphrase that can't be guessed in a very very long time, which means length. Anything less than a really strong passphrase, and you are assuming that the hardware on the phone you are using is so cleverly designed that it will be proof against all current and future attacks.
Or more succinctly, even if you're using one time pads, there'll always be rubber hose cryptanalysis....
